F1.quote: Target Audience: Researchers, universities, research institutes, publishers, vendors, service providers, government, policy makers, funders, and facilities.
F1.claim: the card's summary of whom ORCID serves
F1.checked_against: the card's title and snippet as the registry's cite_list carries them

F2.quote: is a nonproprietary persistent identifier , in the form of an alphanumeric code, to uniquely identify authors and contributors of scholarly communication .
F2.claim: definition: a nonproprietary persistent identifier for authors and contributors of scholarly communication
F2.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F3.quote: This addresses the problem that a particular author's contributions to the scientific literature or humanities publications can be hard to recognize, as most personal names are not unique, they can change ( such as with marriage ), have cultural differences in name order, contain inconsistent use of first-name abbreviations and employ different writing systems .
F3.claim: the name problem the identifier addresses

F4.quote: It provides a persistent identity for humans, similar to tax ID numbers, that are created for content-related entities on digital networks by digital object identifiers (DOIs).
F4.claim: a persistent identity for humans, likened to tax ID numbers and to DOIs

F5.quote: The ORCID system includes a website and services to look up authors and their bibliographic output (and other user-supplied pieces of information).
F5.claim: the system includes lookup of authors and their bibliographic output

F6.quote: multiple persons of the same name could contribute to the same scholarly field, even from the same institutional department
F6.claim: several persons under one name, even in one department

F7.quote: The ORCID organization, ORCID Inc., offers registered users an online means of maintaining "a constantly updated 'digital curriculum vitae' providing a picture of their contributions to science going far beyond the simple publication list", [ 8 ] hosted by ORCID, edited by the user.
F7.claim: the record as a 'digital curriculum vitae', hosted by ORCID, edited by the user

F8.quote: ORCID was first announced in 2009 as a collaborative effort by publishers of scholarly research "to resolve the author name ambiguity problem in scholarly communication".
F8.claim: announced 2009 by publishers to resolve author name ambiguity

F9.quote: A prototype was developed on software adapted from that used by Thomson Reuters for its ResearcherID system.
F9.claim: a prototype adapted from Thomson Reuters's ResearcherID

F10.quote: ORCID, Inc. was incorporated as an independent nonprofit organization in August 2010 in Delaware, United States of America, with an international board of directors.
F10.claim: the operator: ORCID, Inc., a Delaware nonprofit incorporated August 2010

F11.quote: Its executive director, Chris Shillum, was appointed in September 2020; … From 2026, the board is chaired by Heath Marks of the Australian Access Federation
F11.claim: its executive director and board chair

F12.quote: ORCID is freely usable and interoperable with other ID systems.

F13.quote: On 16 October 2012, ORCID launched its registry services

F14.quote: On 15 November 2014, ORCID announced the one-millionth registration. … As of 2 August 2022 [ update ] , ORCID reported 1258 member organizations and 14,727,479 live accounts.
F14.claim: counts: one million registrations (2014); 1258 members and 14,727,479 live accounts (2 August 2022)

F15.quote: publishers that signed this open letter committed to requiring ORCID iDs following specific implementation standards
F15.claim: publishers committed to requiring ORCID iDs (open letter, 2016)

F16.quote: In a 2021 update to the Springer Nature website, they noted that they would thenceforth "support verifying and crediting your [peer] review activity directly from our manuscript submission systems to ORCID".
F16.claim: peer review credited to ORCID records (Springer Nature, 2021)

F17.quote: Formally, ORCID IDs are specified as URLs, [ 27 ] for example, the ORCID ID for Josiah S. Carberry (a fictitious professor used in examples and testing) is https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097
F17.claim: iDs are URLs; the example iD belongs to a fictitious professor used in examples and testing

F18.quote: ORCID IDs are a subset of the International Standard Name Identifier (ISNI), [ 32 ] under the auspices of the International Organization for Standardization (as ISO 27729), and the two organizations are cooperating.
F18.claim: ORCID iDs are a subset of ISNI (ISO 27729)

F19.quote: It is therefore possible for a person to legitimately have both an ISNI and an ORCID ID [ 35 ] [ 36 ] – effectively, two ISNIs.
F19.claim: one person may legitimately hold two ISNIs

F20.quote: Both ORCID and ISNI use 16-character identifiers, … is a MOD 11-2 check digit conforming to the ISO/IEC 7064:2003 standard.
F20.claim: 16-character identifiers with a MOD 11-2 check digit (which may be X)

F21.quote: The organizational members include many research institutions such as Caltech and Cornell University , and publishers such as Elsevier , Springer , Wiley and Nature Publishing Group .

F22.quote: Grant-making bodies such as the Wellcome Trust (a charitable foundation) also mandate that applicants for funding provide an ORCID identifier.

F23.quote: In several countries, consortia, including government bodies as partners, are operating at a national level to implement ORCID.

F24.quote: Both Wikipedia and Wikidata include pages with ORCID identifiers.
F24.claim: Wikipedia and Wikidata carry ORCID identifiers

F25.quote: In October 2015, DataCite , Crossref and ORCID announced that the former organisations would update ORCID records, "when an ORCID identifier is found in newly registered DOI names".
F25.claim: DataCite and Crossref update ORCID records from DOI registrations (2015)

F26.quote: Some ORCID data may also be retrieved as RDF/XML , RDF Turtle , XML or JSON . [ 63 ] [ 64 ] ORCID uses GitHub as its code repository.

F27.quote: Not to be confused with ORCHID .
F27.claim: the hatnote separates ORCID from ORCHID

F28.claim: a category placing the company in Bethesda, Maryland (no sentence of the article states it)

F29.quote: This page was last edited on 19 October 2026, at 03:57
F29.claim: the article was last edited 19 October 2026

F30.quote: ORCID is a non-profit organisation providing researchers with a unique digital identifier. These identifiers can be used by editors, funding agencies, publishers, and institutions to reliably identify individuals in the same way that ISBNs and DOIs identify books and articles.
F30.claim: the organisation provides an identifier used to identify individuals as ISBNs and DOIs identify works
F30.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F31.quote: This removes the risk of confusing your identity with another researcher with the same name.
F31.claim: it removes confusion with a same-named researcher

F32.quote: Springer Nature collaborates with the ORCID organisation to make sure that your research contributions (as authors and peer reviewers) are correctly attributed to you.
F32.claim: the publisher collaborates so contributions are correctly attributed

F33.locus: How can I get an ORCID iD?
F33.quote: On registration, you'll get an ORCID record. You can control what work you include on it and decide who will be able to see it.
F33.claim: the holder controls the works on the record and their visibility

F34.locus: How do I link my Springer Nature account to my ORCID iD?
F34.quote: Only one ORCID account can be linked at a time.
F34.claim: one ORCID account linked at a time

F35.locus: How can I use the ORCID iD as an author?
F35.quote: Unpublished work does not automatically show on your ORCID record, unless it is uploaded to a preprint server, or you manually add it.
F35.claim: what does not reach the record automatically

F36.locus: How do I add my peer reviews to my ORCID record?
F36.quote: When the decision has been made, your review contribution will be shown on your ORCiD record. Only the year of the review and the journal (or book series) title will be shown.
F36.claim: peer review on the record: year and journal only

F37.quote: The Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID) ID is used within NIH and Grants.gov to relate publications to grants.
F37.claim: NIH and Grants.gov use the iD to relate publications to grants

F38.locus: Linking Your ORCID iD, step e
F38.quote: Select the visibility of the information in your ORCID iD record that can contain links to your research activities, affiliations, awards, other versions of your name and more.
F38.claim: the record can contain other versions of the holder's name

F39.quote: The ORCID iD can be linked to only one Commons account.

F40.quote: The ORCID iD is an identifier to enable transparent and trustworthy connections between individuals engaged in research, scholarship, and innovation activities and is tied to an individual researcher's or contributor's name.
F40.claim: the iD is tied to an individual's name

F41.quote: must include an ORCID iD (e.g., orcid.org/0000-0001-2345-6789) to pass NIH validation requirements.
F41.claim: NIH requires the iD for fellowship, career development and trainee profiles

F42.claim: the help page was revised 26 October 2026

F43.quote: ORCID is a non-profit organization, which provides a fully open and interoperable identifier to reliably connect researchers with their research contributions.
F43.claim: a non-profit providing an open identifier connecting researchers with contributions
F43.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F44.quote: The Open Researcher and Contributor ID or ORCID ID is a 16-digit identifier that researchers can register and use for free.

F45.quote: It's a registry of unique persistent identifiers for researchers. It's a hub that connects researchers with their professional activities and contributions.
F45.claim: a registry of identifiers and a hub of contributions
F45.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F46.locus: Challenges using author names to identify individuals: What's in a name?
F46.quote: Names change from marriage, divorce, gender transition, religious conversion, or other circumstances. People use different versions of their name during their career.
F46.claim: why names fail: change of name and several versions of one name

F47.quote: Process that aims to find all publications that belong to a given author and distinguish them from publications of other authors who share the same name.

F48.locus: Why you need an ORCID ID
F48.quote: ORCID is not for profit: your data is not tracked or sold. Own and control your own record: choose which information is private and which is shared.
F48.claim: not for profit; the holder controls the record

F49.locus: Why you need an ORCID ID
F49.quote: ORCID is supported and increasingly required by major funders, publishers, societies, and research organizations.

F50.claim: the guide was last updated 2 June 2025

F51.quote: What is ORCID? Ultimate Guide to Researcher Identification
F51.claim: a video titled as a guide to researcher identification
F51.checked_against: the card's title and snippet as the registry's cite_list carries them

F52.quote: An ORCID iD is a free, permanent 16-character identifier that reliably connects you to your research — no matter how common your name is or how it is spelled.
F52.claim: a free, permanent 16-character identifier, whatever the name or its spelling
F52.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F53.quote: Just as a DOI permanently identifies an article, an ORCID iD permanently identifies you and links to a record of your works, affiliations and funding.
F53.claim: the iD identifies the person as a DOI identifies an article

F54.quote: Disambiguation — it separates you from other researchers with the same name, and from variations of your own name (initials, maiden names, transliterations).
F54.claim: disambiguation from others and from variations of one's own name

F55.quote: It follows you — through job changes, name changes and career moves.

F56.locus: FAQ: What does an ORCID iD look like?
F56.quote: It is a 16-character iD, written as four groups of four — for example, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097. The final character is a check digit that may be a number or the letter X.
F56.claim: the format, with the example iD given without its holder

F57.locus: FAQ: Does ORCID make my personal information public?
F57.quote: Your 16-character iD is public, but you decide what information is attached to it.
F57.claim: the iD public, its information the holder's choice

F58.quote: Yes. Registering for an ORCID iD is completely free for researchers, and it takes only a few minutes at orcid.org.

F59.quote: explains how to keep its publication list in step with your ORCID record by hand.
F59.claim: a Google Scholar list kept in step with the record by hand

F60.quote: By Directive Editorial Team, Directive Publications
F60.claim: the guide is the publisher's editorial team's

F61.locus: card title (video, 3:13; the card's own title is 'YouTube')
F61.claim: a Northwestern University Libraries video whose card carries no title of its own
F61.checked_against: the card's title and snippet as the registry's cite_list carries them

F62.quote: ORCID, which stands for Open Researcher and Contributor ID, is a global, not-for-profit organization sustained by fees from our member organizations.
F62.claim: self-description: a global not-for-profit sustained by member fees

F63.quote: We are community-built and governed by a Board of Directors representative of our membership with wide stakeholder representation.
F63.claim: governed by a board representative of its membership

F64.quote: ORCID’s vision is a world where all who participate in research, scholarship, and innovation are uniquely identified and connected to their contributions across disciplines, borders, and time.
F64.claim: the vision: everyone in research uniquely identified

F65.quote: The ORCID iD: a unique, persistent identifier free of charge to researchers … An ORCID record connected to the ORCID iD, and
F65.claim: the iD and the record connected to it
F65.lineage: what it is: a persistent identifier for researchers

F66.quote: Our strategic focus for 2026–2029 is to expand the value and scope of ORCID as a verifiable identity and contribution data hub
F66.claim: plan 2026–2029: a verifiable identity and contribution data hub

F67.quote: ORCID will work to support the creation of a permanent, clear, and unambiguous record of research and scholarly communication by enabling reliable attribution of authors and contributors.
F67.claim: founding principle: an unambiguous record by reliable attribution

F68.quote: Researchers will control the defined privacy settings of their own ORCID record data.
F68.claim: researchers control their records' privacy settings

F69.quote: All data contributed to ORCID by researchers or claimed by them will be available in standard formats for free download (subject to the researchers’ own privacy settings) that are updated once a year and released under a CC0 waiver.
F69.claim: public data released yearly under a CC0 waiver

F70.quote: Participation in ORCID is open to any organization that has an interest in research and scholarly communications.
F70.claim: participation open to any organization with an interest in research

F71.quote: We are guided by the principles of privacy and researcher control and the vision of identifier-enabled research information infrastructure.
F71.claim: privacy and researcher control as principles

F72.quote: has reserved a block of identifiers for use by ORCID, [ 32 ] [ 33 ] in the range 0000-0001-5000-0007 to 0000-0003-5000-0001.
F72.claim: ISNI reserved a block of identifiers for ORCID, 0000-0001-5000-0007 to 0000-0003-5000-0001

F73.claim: the infobox's check-digit example, an iD beginning 0009

F74.quote: It saves time — many submission and grant systems auto-fill your details from your ORCID record.
F74.claim: submission and grant systems auto-fill from the record

F75.quote: Set your visibility preferences — you control what is public, trusted or private.
